title: Georgia Father Found Guilty of Murder in Death of Toddler Left in Hot Car
text: With local television programming interrupted and a camera fixed on the defendant’s emotionless face, a father was convicted of murder on Monday for causing the death of his young son by deliberately leaving him in a hot car more than two years ago. A jury in southeast Georgia, where the case was heard because of intense pretrial publicity in Atlanta, found the man, Justin Ross Harris, 35, guilty on eight counts, including malice murder and cruelty to children. Mr. Harris, who at times looked downward as the verdict was read in Brunswick, could face life in prison for the death of his son, Cooper. The verdict, which came on the fourth day of jury deliberations, ended the suspense of a trial that opened on Oct. 3, and it brought to a close nearly 29 months of sordid allegations and scrambled loyalties. How Cooper died was not in dispute: Mr. Harris left him in a Hyundai Tucson while he was at work as a software engineer at Home Depot on June 18, 2014. It was left to jurors to decide whether he had acted maliciously. The way Cooper died is heartbreakingly familiar: at least 39 children in the United States have died of “vehicular heatstroke” this year, according to statistics gathered by a San Jose State University researcher. But the case against Mr. Harris stood out because of how severe the charges were and because of the state’s argument that he was eager to be free of his responsibilities to his family. “This killer’s heart abandoned this child long before he died,” Charles P. Boring, an assistant district attorney, said in his closing argument. “This defendant’s heart abandoned this child when he left him to die a terrible death in that car.”

title: Cuban Man Faces Deportation After Posing as Border Patrol Agent
text: A federal judge in south Texas sentenced a Cuban national who posed as a U.S. Border Patrol agent to prison. The Cuban man tried to scam a confidential informant into paying him $7,000 in return for permanent resident status documents. U.S. District Court Judge Randy Crane said he needed to protect the community from Euginio Augustin, a Cuban national with Legal Permanent Resident status in the U.S., because of his criminal history of theft and fraud. However, the judge sentenced the man to only 18 months in prison, according to a statement from the Department of Justice’s Southern District of Texas. The maximum penalty for impersonating a federal agent or officer (18 U.S. Code § 912) is three years in prison. Court records obtained by Breitbart Texas showed that Augustin introduced himself to a confidential informant (CI) who claimed to be an illegal alien. The Cuban man told the CI that he was a U.S. Border Patrol agent and said he could get Legal Permanent Resident (LPR) documents for him in return for $7,000. In a call ahead of the meeting, he told the CI he would need a copy of his Mexican visa and two passport photos, claiming those were the documents he needed to obtain the LPR documents. The CI handed the suspect a down payment of $2,800 along with the requested documents. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement special agents from the Office of Professional Responsibility arrested Augustin as he left the meeting. According to the DOJ statement, he had solicited bribes from multiple people seeking legal status in the U.S. Officials said they expect an ICE Enforcement Removal officer to deport him to Cuba once he completes his sentence in a federal prison.

title: Clinton lawyer criticizes FBI after release of email search warrant
text: The FBI behaved inappropriately when it announced, days before the Nov. 8 presidential election, that it was reviving its investigation into Hillary Clinton’s private email setup, Clinton’s lawyer said, pointing to search warrant documents made public on Tuesday. The sharp criticism from Clinton attorney David Kendall came after documents related to an October search warrant targeting emails involving the Democratic presidential nominee were released in federal court in Manhattan. The warrant was issued two days after Federal Bureau of Investigation Director James Comey told Congress in a letter on Oct. 28 about newly discovered emails that appeared “pertinent” to his agency’s probe. Comey’s letter put fresh attention on Clinton’s use of the server during her time as secretary of state from 2009 to 2013 and roiled the campaign 11 days before the election, which was won by Republican Donald Trump. Clinton has blamed Comey and his letter for her defeat. In an affidavit unsealed on Tuesday, an FBI agent said there was “probable cause” to believe that emails involving Clinton were among “thousands” found on a laptop in an unrelated probe that contained U.S. State Department correspondence. But the documents gave no sign that, at the time of Comey’s letter, the FBI had any evidence that any of the emails found on a laptop involved classified communications with Clinton. Kendall said the documents demonstrated the “extraordinary impropriety” of Comey’s letter, which “produced devastating but predictable damage politically and which was both legally unauthorized and factually unnecessary.” The FBI declined to comment. The laptop belonged to former Democratic U.S. Representative Anthony Weiner, the estranged husband of Clinton aide Huma Abedin, who had been the subject of an investigation following a report about cellphone and online messages he sent to a 15-year-old girl.

title: Factbox: Grading Donald Trump's first 100 days
text: U.S. President Donald Trump came into office on Jan. 20 with a long list of promises for his first 100 days, and his record so far has been mixed. Below are the main issues he has faced and what he has accomplished ahead of his 100th day on Saturday. Repealing and replacing the 2010 Affordable Care Act, President Barack Obama’s signature domestic policy, was one of the central promises of Trump’s 2016 election campaign. It is also among the biggest failures of his first 100 days. A House of Representatives bill was pulled in late March when Republicans could not gather enough votes to pass it, even though they control the chamber. A revised plan this week has won support from the House Freedom Caucus, the conservative bloc that helped defeat the original bill. That boosts the odds of a deal in the House, although it is not clear whether it can win over enough moderate Republicans, and it would run into tougher obstacles in the Senate. Trump repeatedly promised the biggest tax overhaul since the 1980s. This week he put forward legislation to cut the corporate tax rate to 15 percent from 35 percent, lower the top personal income tax rate to 35 percent, repeal the inheritance tax and temporarily cut the rate on overseas profits brought back to the United States. However, the plan is vague, and even senior Republican lawmakers said it offered only “guideposts” for legislative changes. Trump’s foreign policy has seen major shifts. Russia: During the campaign Trump spoke admiringly of Russian President Vladimir Putin and signalled that he wanted a rapprochement with Moscow. But the administration has been unable to shake off a controversy that has prompted a congressional investigation into Russian meddling in the 2016 election, including possible links between Trump’s campaign and Moscow.

title: EU leaders adopt European social standards in bid to win over voters
text: European Union leaders proclaimed a set of 20 social rights on Friday, in an effort to make the EU more attractive to voters and to counter growing eurosceptic sentiment across the bloc. The set of social rights, backed by all EU governments and institutions, sets out what the EU considers the foundations of fair and well-functioning modern labor markets and welfare systems. It covers principles ranging from equal access to jobs and fair working conditions and wages to social protection, unemployment benefits and training. “Our Union has always been a social project at heart. It is more than just a single market, more than money, more than the euro. It is about our values and the way we want to live,” European Commission President Jean-Claude Juncker said. “Today we assert our common values and commit ourselves to a set of 20 principles and rights. From the right to fair wages to the right to health care; from lifelong learning, a better work-life balance and gender equality to minimum income,” he said. Recent elections in Germany, France, Austria and the Czech Republic, in which populist parties did well, have shown that citizens have lost confidence in governments or in the European Union. “There is certainly a need to respond,” a senior EU official said. Britain’s decision last year to leave the EU acted as a wake-up call for the bloc and prompted it to think about the way forward, including placing more emphasis on social policies. “I think people believe there’s been maybe an excessive focus in recent years on economic matters, banking, and we want to re-fire the engine of social Europe, advancing things like equality, workers rights, pension rights and other things,” Irish Prime Minister Leo Varadkar said.

title: The Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: A desperate escape
text: Two months after militant attacks set off a military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine State, the world’s fastest-growing humanitarian crisis shows no sign of easing. This week thousands more Rohingya Muslim refugees crossed the border into neighboring Bangladesh, escaping hunger and a campaign of attacks by Myanmar security forces and Buddhist mobs that the United Nations has described as ethnic cleansing. Exhausted, hungry and destitute, they join more than 600,000 people who fled earlier from what the military calls clearance operations in Rohingya villages following the Aug. 25 attacks by Rohingya militants. They have crossed land borders, rivers and treacherous seas to find refuge in crowded camps in Bangladesh, itself a poor country that, together with international aid agencies, is struggling to cope with the influx. This multimedia essay combines graphics, pictures and video to show how the crisis unfolded, the exodus of the Rohingya and their lives as refugees in Bangladesh, including the graphic “A Desperate Escape.”

title: Kenyan court orders access to poll returns in bid to annul election
text: Kenya’s Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the country’s election board must give the parties challenging President Uhuru Kenyatta’s win in last month’s presidential election access to the election returns. The petitioners, a former lawmaker and two human rights activists, must be given immediate access to the original vote tally forms and a copy of the voter register, the judges said. They turned down a request for access to the electronic devices used to count votes. The legal challenges follow the court’s decision to annul Kenyatta’s August victory and order a new election, an unprecedented step in Africa. The current proceedings may be the final opportunity for legal scrutiny of the second election, which took place on Oct. 26. The long-running political crisis has raised fears for the stability of the east African nation, a regional hub for trade, diplomacy and security. The court is working to a tight timetable. It must rule on the two petitions by Nov. 20. If the result is upheld, Kenyatta will be sworn in on Nov. 28. Chief Justice David Maraga told the petitioners to file a report on what they find in the returns by Thursday afternoon. Following Wednesday’s ruling, lawyers for the petitioners started presenting their cases, arguing among other things that the outcome of the poll is void because the election board did not hold fresh nominations after the earlier vote was invalidated. “Our position is you cannot have a fresh presidential election without a fresh round of nominations,” said Benjamin Musyoki, a lawyer for former legislator Harun Mwau.
